extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations and communications (undergraduate/introductory level)
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and evaluate Grunig & Hunt’s four public relations models (press agency/publicity, public information, two-way asymmetric, two-way symmetric), their practical applications, ethical implications, and criticisms, with examples and a case-study perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agency/Publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Attraction by the media due to the activities of an organization (press agency/publicist model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-way, publicity-focused communication aimed at gaining media attention; traditional/traditional mass-communication techniques such as press conferences and news releases are typical; emphasis is on generating publicity rather than mutual understanding or policy change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public information
rubrics_metrics.description: The means by which information is generated and disseminated to the public about an organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one-way managerial approach where the primary concern is accurate and efficient distribution of information: timing, channels, quality control, and ensuring information reaches the right audiences. Managers act to manage the transfer of information and make a positive presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way Asymmetric communication
rubrics_metrics.description: A system that allows an organization to communicate with the public and receive feedback about the conveyed information, but the organization does not change its policies in response; feedback is used to persuade or influence the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication is ostensibly two-way but unequal — feedback is collected to design more effective persuasive messages rather than to negotiate change. Anti-pattern: treating feedback as data for manipulation rather than grounds for policy change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way Symmetric communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Free and equal movement of information between the organization and the public, implying mutual influence, negotiation, and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative 'ideal' model for PR excellence: promotes negotiation and fair resolution of problems, mutual adjustment of organization and public, and ethical practice. Guidance notes: often cited as rarely used in practice; criticized as over-idealized but seen as central to ethical, managerial PR and building stronger relationships with publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR excellence characteristics (symmetrical, idealistic, critical, managerial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grunig’s assertion that for PR to be excellent it must be 'symmetrical, idealistic, critical, and managerial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are normative attributes used to judge whether PR practice is exemplary. Caveat: critics argue this list is over-idealized, prescriptive, and may not reflect practical organizational realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand social, cultural and economic context
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations must understand the social, economic and cultural setting of their customers to increase effectiveness and reach cross-cultural markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing communication, account for cultural differences, language barriers, values, and beliefs through mutual communication; use this understanding to tailor products, messages, and approaches for different markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and fair conflict resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems between an organization and its publics should be resolved in a fair way, with ethics central to mutual understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-way symmetrical model emphasizes negotiation, ethical assessment of public attitudes, and organizational adaptation; ethical practice is necessary for trust-building and reshaping organizational behavior in response to publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of interactive media and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactive media (e.g., web features) facilitate two-way communication, stakeholder participation, transparency and equality in decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: employ interactive channels to solicit feedback and increase transparency. Examples cited: Singapore and Malaysia use web interactivity to enhance government and stakeholder dialogue. Transparency supports democratic participation and improved stakeholder relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managers’ role as controllers/mediators of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations managers are responsible for controlling and managing communication between an organization and its publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks include conveying the right information to the right people at the right time, tracking communication, ensuring quality control, and acting as organizational spokespersons. Balance required between control and openness depending on model used.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single model is universally superior; use interchangeably
rubrics_metrics.description: All four models have value; organizations should use traditional one-way and two-way models interchangeably rather than assuming one is always superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: select model(s) appropriate to context and objectives. Anti-pattern: rigid adherence to one model irrespective of situational demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and critiques of the models (over-idealization, hybrid paradigms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grunig & Hunt’s models — especially two-way symmetrical — have been criticized as over-idealized, hybrid constructions drawn from varying system paradigms and lacking clear practical guidance for management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating applicability, consider empirical evidence that two-way symmetry is rarely used; assess theoretical hybridity and contradictions; be cautious about treating the models as prescriptive templates without adapting to organizational realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for open or adaptive organizational systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual understanding requires an open system, but real organizations may need adaptive systems that account for hierarchy and management structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement communication systems that balance openness with organizational constraints: adapt processes to enable negotiation while respecting necessary managerial structures. Anti-pattern: assuming ideal open systems are easily implementable in hierarchical organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective communication channels and stakeholder engagement (practical execution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective PR depends on proper communication channels, appropriate interview and research methods (individual/group), and active stakeholder engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case-study evidence: poor interview methods and lack of proper channels hinder understanding and cross-functional communication. Practical guidance: design robust channels, employ appropriate qualitative methods, and ensure stakeholder voices inform decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of PR professionals as organizational spokespersons
rubrics_metrics.description: PR professionals act as spokespersons of organizations, mediating between the organization and publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They should manage messaging, choose appropriate channels, and be accountable for both disseminating information and facilitating feedback. Consider ethical obligations when acting as spokespersons.
